title: Foraging elderflower: harvest, ID, and preparation
subtitle: May and June flower heads for cordial and fritters
excerpt: Elder produces its cream flower heads in May and June along UK hedgerows and woodland edges. The flowers are edible and make cordial, fritters, and elderflower champagne. The raw berries that follow in autumn are not safe to eat and must be cooked first.
sourceNotes: Richard Mabey, Food for Free (1972); John Wright, The Forager's Calendar (2019); BSBI species accounts for Sambucus nigra; Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.

glossaryTerms.definition: Matching three independent visual, scent, or habitat features before eating any wild plant. All three must match; a single mismatch means stop.
A wild plant that resembles an edible species closely enough to cause misidentification. Many look-alikes are toxic.
The specific habitat type where a wild plant grows, used as one of the three identification features.

content.text: Elder (Sambucus nigra) produces flat-topped heads of tiny cream flowers from late May through June along UK hedgerows, woodland edges, roadsides, and waste ground. The flowers are edible and make cordial, elderflower champagne, and fritters. The raw unripe berries that follow in autumn can cause nausea; they need cooking before use. Verify your identification before eating; if in doubt, do not eat.
Apply the
rule-of-three identification
: confirm (1) the flat-topped cream flower head with a sweet, heavy scent, (2) the opposite pairs of pinnate leaves with five to seven leaflets, and (3) the hedgerow, woodland-edge, or roadside
foraging zone
. All three must match.
ID features
Flower head: flat-topped (corymb), 10 to 25 cm across, dozens of tiny cream flowers. Sweet, heavy scent. If it smells unpleasant or musty, leave it.
Leaves: pinnate, five to seven oval leaflets with toothed edges, arranged in opposite pairs along the stem. Crushed leaves smell unpleasant.
Bark: grey, corky, furrowed on older stems. Pith inside the young stems is white and spongy.
Season: flowers from late May through June. Berries form from August through September.
Poisonous look-alikes
Two plants produce similar white flower clusters and share the elder's hedgerow habitat. Both are toxic
look-alikes
Hemlock (Conium maculatum): tall, often spotted purple stems, fern-like leaves, unpleasant musty smell. The flower clusters are smaller and dome-shaped, not flat-topped. Extremely toxic.

Hemlock water dropwort (Oenanthe crocata): grows near water with bright white flat-topped flower clusters and carrot-like leaves. No elder-style pinnate leaflets. Extremely toxic; one of the UK's most dangerous plants.
When and how to harvest

Pick flower heads from late May through mid-June. Choose heads where the majority of florets are fully open and the scent is sweet and clean. Avoid heads that are browning at the edges or smell cat-like or unpleasant; those are past their best. Cut the stem about 2 cm below the head with scissors. Take from several different elder plants and leave the majority of heads to set fruit for wildlife.
After harvesting

Use the same day or the day after; the flowers begin to lose their scent and brown quickly. Shake gently to dislodge insects. Do not wash the flower heads if making cordial, because washing removes the wild yeasts needed for elderflower champagne; for other uses, a brief cold rinse is fine. For cordial, steep the heads in hot sugar syrup with lemon zest and juice for 24 hours, then strain through a cloth into sterilised bottles.
Legal and ethical

The Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 and Theft Act 1968 allow collection of flowers from hedgerows and common land for personal use. Private land requires the landowner's permission. Leave at least two-thirds of the heads on any tree you visit so the berries can ripen for birds and other wildlife.

rows.symptom: Flower heads smell musty or of cat
rows.cause: Heads are past their peak, or the plant is not elder but a look-alike
rows.fix: Do not use heads with an unpleasant smell. Fresh elder flower has a clean, sweet, slightly citrus scent. If the smell is wrong, move to a different plant.

rows.symptom: Cordial is bitter rather than sweet
rows.cause: Too many stems included, or heads were past their peak
rows.fix: Strip the individual florets from the larger stems before steeping; the main stem adds bitterness. Use only heads at peak freshness, fully open and fragrant.

rows.symptom: Uncertain whether the plant is elder or hemlock
rows.cause: Both grow as tall shrubs in hedgerows with flat-topped white flower clusters
rows.fix: Check the leaves: elder has large pinnate leaflets with toothed edges; hemlock has finely divided, fern-like leaves. Hemlock has a distinctly unpleasant musty smell. If uncertain, do not use.
